Agentic workloads are demanding more from inference systems. AI agents carry growing conversation histories across turns and generate a mix of reasoning, tool calls, and responses. Inference systems must support users at scale while remaining responsive.

MLPerf Endpoints v1.0 evaluates this balance between serving capacity and responsiveness using coding and enterprise workflows through API endpoints. During performance runs, generated tool calls and workflow intent are checked against reference values. Separate SWE-bench Verified evaluations assess end-to-end task-solving capability. These checks evaluate whether faster serving preserves model quality.

In MLPerf Endpoints v1.0, provisional NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 results show over 10x the throughput per kilowatt of provisioned power of NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 at a shared minimum end-to-end interactivity of 50 tokens per second per user.1

This post presents the benchmark results and outlines the hardware and software optimizations used in the submissions.

The serving demands of multi-turn agentic AI

The MLPerf Endpoints v1.0 dataset captures these workload characteristics: coding trajectories accumulate history over many turns, while enterprise workflows reuse shared instructions, tool definitions, and business rules. Higher throughput per kilowatt enables organizations to run more agents simultaneously within the same power budget while meeting the same responsiveness requirement. At low concurrency, faster responses reduce inference wait times for latency-sensitive agentic tasks.

Hardware and software optimizations for agentic inference

NVIDIA Rubin GPUs combine HBM4 memory, NVIDIA Tensor Cores, and sixth-generation NVIDIA NVLink to support the demands of agentic inference. HBM4 enables rapid access to model weights and conversation state, Tensor Cores accelerate matrix operations, and NVLink supports communication across GPUs. Context-aware serving and model-specific kernels build on these capabilities to reuse prior work, independently optimize prefill and decode, and accelerate token generation—translating hardware advances into greater inference capacity and faster interactions.

Context-aware serving and model-specific optimizations improve inference performance

Agentic workloads repeatedly reuse conversation history while adding new instructions and tool results. Efficient serving must preserve reusable state, distribute requests across workers, and accommodate the different execution requirements of prompt processing and token generation. Prefix caching, state reuse, and NVIDIA Dynamo routing help reduce redundant computation and balance serving load, while disaggregated serving supports independent optimization of prefill and decode.

Figure 3 summarizes how context-aware serving and model-specific GPU execution support agentic inference.

Figure 3. Context-aware serving and optimized GPU execution for agentic inference

Kimi K3, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B also have distinct architectures that benefit from targeted GPU execution improvements. Model-specific kernels, fusion, optimized memory access, and speculative verification reduce data movement and execution overhead. Table 2 summarizes how these serving and execution techniques work together across the three models.

Software optimizations improve context reuse, serving efficiency, and GPU execution

More productive infrastructure for agentic AI

Agentic inference performance depends on co-design across hardware, system architecture, and serving software. The provisional MLPerf Endpoints v1.0 results show how the Vera Rubin platform brings these capabilities together to address the demands of agentic workloads and create more capacity to serve users and scale applications.
